visual.text: The best ten minutes of your day are not in a car.
Walk to School Week — leave the back seat and use your feet.
Four students in uniform stroll along a covered walkway, laughing and sharing a packet of biscuits. Behind them, a long line of cars waits outside the school gate.

Every morning, the road outside our gate fills with cars, and half of us arrive sleepy and silent. For one week, try something different. Get off the bus a stop early, or ask to be dropped at the park. Walk the rest with a friend. You will reach class awake, with a story to tell.

visual.title: How it works
items: Collect a stamp card from your form teacher
Walk in on any morning and have it stamped at the gate before 7.20 am
Five stamps earn you a breakfast set from the canteen
The class with the most stamps chooses the music at Friday’s assembly

visual.text: “I used to scroll on my phone all the way to school. Now I walk with my neighbour, and we have actually become friends.” — Hui Min, Secondary 3
Live too far away to walk? Join a Walking Bus from Block 204 or the MRT station, led by prefects, at 6.55 am.
Pick up your stamp card on Monday

questions.text: How does the picture support the message of the poster?

scheme.answer: It shows the students who walk laughing and enjoying one another’s company while the cars are stuck in a queue, so walking looks more pleasant than being driven.
accept: It contrasts cheerful students on foot with a traffic jam at the gate, which makes walking seem the better way to come to school.

seeds.text: It shows the students who walk are happy and having fun together, while the cars are all stuck in a jam, so walking looks better than going by car.
The walkers are laughing with their friends but the cars behind cannot move, so it makes us feel walking is the nicer way to get to school.
It shows that students should share their food with their friends.
The picture makes the poster more colourful and attractive.
It shows that there are too many cars in Singapore.

questions.text: The poster is written for the students of one school. Give one piece of evidence from the poster that shows this.

scheme.answer: It says ‘our gate’ and ‘half of us’, so the writer and the readers belong to the same school.
accept: Stamp cards are collected from ‘your form teacher’.
The rewards are a breakfast set from the canteen and choosing the music at Friday’s assembly.
It quotes Hui Min, a Secondary 3 student.
The Walking Bus is led by prefects.
It is put up by the Student Council.

seeds.text: It uses 'our gate' and 'half of us', which shows the writer is talking to people in the same school.
Students have to collect the stamp card from their form teacher, and only students have form teachers.
The prize is a breakfast set from the school canteen.
It says the best ten minutes of your day are not in a car.
The poster uses simple words that are easy to understand.

questions.text: Why does the poster include the information about the Walking Bus?

scheme.answer: It shows students who live far away that they can still take part, by walking the last stretch in a group.
accept: So that students who live too far to walk from home do not feel left out and have a way to join in.

seeds.text: So that students who stay far from school can still join by walking part of the way with the group.
Some students cannot walk all the way from home, so this gives them a way to take part too and not be left out.
To tell students that there is a new bus service to the school.
To give students more information about the week.
To show that prefects are responsible students.

questions.text: Look at the headline: ‘The best ten minutes of your day are not in a car.’ What does it suggest about walking to school?

scheme.answer: Walking to school can be the most enjoyable part of a student’s day, much better than sitting in a car.
accept: A short walk to school is something to look forward to, and students who are driven miss out on it.

seeds.text: It suggests that walking to school is very enjoyable and can even be the best part of the whole day, better than being driven.
Students who sit in a car are missing out, because the short walk is actually the nicest time of their day.
It suggests that it takes exactly ten minutes to walk to school.
The best ten minutes of your day are not in a car.
It suggests that cars are dangerous for students.
It suggests something about how students travel to school.
